newsitem.title: USA: Running a restaurant not as simple as you think.
newsitem.headline: Running a restaurant not as simple as you think.

text.p: It seems just about anyone who's a good cook thinks they can make a go of a restaurant business. But an expert in the industry says it's not that simple, and the key to success or failure actually starts six months before the first meal is ordered.

"One of the things that's important is to realise that the failure rate in restaurants is so high. Fifty percent fail in the first year, and after five years, only 25 percent survive," said Isidore Kharasch, president of Hospitality Works Inc., a Chicago-based restaurant consulting firm.

His company has worked with 175 foodservice operations in 20 states and five foreign countries. Many have been start-ups, but it also deals with companies operating in Chapter 11 bankruptcy, as well as those on the verge of filing for protection from creditors.

"Fifty percent of our business now is made up of customers that we go in and save -- they're either in Chapter 11 or on the brink," said Kharasch. The other half of the business is a mixture of training seminars and new business development.
Kharasch gets great satisfaction from helping entrepreneurs get it right from the beginning, or even reaching the conclusion that the restaurant business is not for them.

"We believe that if a restaurant is going to fail, they fail six months before they're going to open," he said. "They set themselves up for failure, through unrealistic expectations, poor design, being undercapitalized and not providing training for their staff."
First of all, Karasch noted, the restaurant business requires "an intense, intense amount of hours -- more hours than you could dream of."
He recalled how a husband and wife decided to open a small breakfast restaurant next to a building they owned.

"After the first week, the wife broke down in tears from exhaustion," he said. "Being able to cook is helpful, but being able to put in the amount of hours is just almost unbearable, especially for someone who's older. It's very intense. It's more than people think it's going to be."
As part of the planning process, Kharasch and his clients look closely at the costs involved in launching and maintaining a profitable restaurant operation.
"We forecast how much it will cost to build an operation," he said. "But more importantly, we forecast what a customer will have to do in sales to be profitable."

The amount of money you have to generate to make an operation successful is probably much higher than you think, he said. "You would have to keep your rent at about 5 percent of your gross sales to really be successful. We look at 10 percent as the high side.
"We'd say, 'If you want to put this restaurant on this street, is it feasible that you're going to have enough people walking through your door every day?'"
For example, he said, a husband and wife wanted to open a bakery on Chicago's high-priced Michigan Avenue. The initial investment was to be over $1 million.

"When we broke it down to show how many customers they would need, it was 600 people spending $7 each daily six days a week just to keep them above water," Kharasch said. "They decided not to go into the business."

For those who decide to go through with it, Kharasch's company will help with everything from developing a business plan to designing a kitchen, planning a menu, recruiting a chef and training management, bar and service staff.
By now, you may be thinking that even if you've got a great idea for an eatery, it would be money well spent to confer with an expert.
How much might that cost?
If you contact Kharasch, he'll talk to you briefly in person or by phone (773-880-8833) for free and then put together a proposal outlining what his company can do for you, under one price.

"If all a client needed was some of the basic information, we would talk and I would put them on the clock for an hour at about $150 an hour," he said. "If they decide to go ahead, we would need to spend 10 to 15 hours putting together a business plan, and that would cost about $1,500 to $2,000.
At the opposite end of the spectrum, the firm is putting together a package that includes everything to get a 9,000-square-foot, 250-seat restaurant started.

It includes a startup study, menus, recipes, lease negotiations, market analysis and planning, kitchen design, interior design, advertising and public relations. For such a package, Karasch will charge about $90,000.
"Sometimes that first hour is enough to turn them off to the business," Kharasch said. But he figures that is time well spent for both client and consultant.
"This year alone, we've turned about five people away from the restaurant industry, and we consider those some of our greatest success stories," he said.
"They are the kind of people who have way too much money and would never go to the bank until the last minute. They'd end up losing a lot of money."
